Vocational speed bin distributions for single-unit short-haul vehicles Figure 50 simply shows the speed distributions for the CE-CERT and FleetDNA refuse trucks, as only one vocation existed for each. When a road-day combination did not contain sufficient data, it was left off the plot, such as FleetDNA refuse driving on urban freeways on weekends or CE- CERT refuse driving on urban other roads on weekends. On both urban road types on weekdays, FleetDNA spends more time in speed bin 2 (midpoint at 5 mph) and less time at speeds above 30 mph compared to CE-CERT; for example, the 60-mph peak on urban freeways on weekdays is much less pronounced for FleetDNA than for CE-CERT. 61 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 50. Vocational speed bin distributions for refuse trucks Lastly, we display the vocational speed distributions within transit buses of FleetDNA and CE- CERT data sets. The mass transit vocation comes from FleetDNA and is the only vocation with robust data on urban other roads on weekdays, while the other two vocations appear only in CE- CERT data. Urban diesel hybrid buses spend the most time in the high-speed bin at 60 mph compared to the other vocations, while mass transit buses spend the least time at high speeds on urban freeways. Between the three vocations, we see more alignment on urban other roads on weekdays, with transit express buses spending more time in speed bins above 25 mph and urban diesel hybrid buses spending the most time in speed bin 2 (centered at 5 mph). 62 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Vocational speed bin distributions for transit buses As seen in the source type analysis of this section, by aggregating data over all hours of the day, we were able to include additional speed distributions, such as urban freeways on weekends for single-unit short-haul vehicles. We could also possibly add combination-unit short-haul rural weekday data and transit bus urban weekend data, despite counts being slightly shy of robust data cutoffs. Refuse truck urban weekday data could possibly be combined with weekend data to augment low data availability that remained for urban weekend refuse data even after aggregation across hours.
